questions.stem: To operationalise a variable means to:
options: decide whether it is the independent or the dependent variable
remove its influence on the results by keeping it constant
predict the direction in which it will change the results
define exactly how it will be manipulated or measured in the study
questions.explanation: Operationalising turns an abstract variable such as 'stress' into something observable and measurable, for example heart rate or a score on a stress questionnaire. Keeping a variable constant is controlling it, which is a different step.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying whether caffeine improves alertness. Which is the best operationalised dependent variable?
options: How alert the participants seem to the researcher
Whether participants drink coffee or decaffeinated coffee
The participants' general level of energy during the day
Mean reaction time in milliseconds on a computer task
questions.explanation: An operationalised dependent variable states precisely how it will be measured, such as mean reaction time in milliseconds. 'How alert they seem' is vague and subjective, and the type of coffee is the independent variable.

questions.stem: Which statement is a null hypothesis?
options: Sleep affects how many words participants recall from a list of 20 words
There will be no difference in recall between participants who sleep and those who stay awake
Participants who sleep will recall more words than participants who stay awake
Participants who stay awake will recall more words than participants who sleep
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis states that there is no difference or relationship between the variables, and is what inferential statistics test against. The other statements predict an effect, so they are alternative hypotheses.

questions.stem: In an independent groups design:
options: the same participants take part in every condition
participants are paired on a key variable before testing
variables are measured but not manipulated by the researcher
different participants take part in each condition
questions.explanation: Each participant is in only one condition, so groups are compared with each other. Using the same participants in every condition is repeated measures, and pairing participants is a matched participants design.

questions.stem: A researcher ranks 40 participants by IQ score, pairs the top two, the next two and so on, then randomly places one of each pair in each condition. This is:
options: a matched participants design
a repeated measures design
an independent groups design using convenience sampling
a quasi-experimental design using random sampling
questions.explanation: In a matched participants design, participants are paired on a variable likely to affect the results, and one member of each pair is allocated to each condition. This controls that participant variable while avoiding order effects.

questions.stem: In a repeated measures study of noise and concentration, half the participants do the quiet condition first and half do the noisy condition first. This procedure is called:
options: counterbalancing
random sampling
double-blind testing
standardisation
questions.explanation: Counterbalancing varies the order of conditions so that order effects such as practice and fatigue are spread evenly across them rather than favouring one condition. Random sampling concerns how participants are selected, not the order of conditions.

questions.stem: Researchers compare the memory scores of people who already have insomnia with those of good sleepers. Why is this a quasi-experiment rather than a true experiment?
options: The study has a control group, which true experiments never include
The dependent variable is measured on an ordinal level of measurement
Participants cannot be randomly allocated, because the groups exist already
No independent variable is involved, because sleep is only measured
questions.explanation: In a quasi-experiment the independent variable is a pre-existing characteristic, here insomnia, so the researcher cannot randomly allocate people to conditions. Groups may then differ in other ways, which weakens conclusions about cause.

questions.stem: A researcher records students' daily screen time and their anxiety scores, then calculates how strongly the two variables are related. Which type of research is this?
options: a quasi-experiment
a repeated measures experiment
an independent groups experiment
correlational research
questions.explanation: Correlational research measures two or more variables as they occur and examines the relationship between them, without manipulating either. It can show an association but not cause.

questions.stem: A psychologist sits at the edge of a playground and records how often children share toys, without interacting with them. This is an example of:
options: a matched participants experiment
a quasi-experiment
correlational research
observational research
questions.explanation: Observational research records behaviour as it occurs, often in natural settings, without manipulating variables. The psychologist needs a clear operational definition of sharing so that observations are reliable.

questions.stem: Participants record their favourite music genre: pop, rock, classical or hip hop. What level of measurement is this?
options: interval
ratio
nominal
ordinal
questions.explanation: Nominal data are categories with no order or numerical value. A genre is simply a label, so the data can be counted but not ranked or averaged.

questions.stem: Participants rate their mood on a scale: 1 = very unhappy, 2 = unhappy, 3 = neutral, 4 = happy, 5 = very happy. Which level of measurement is most accurate?
options: nominal, because each number is only a label for a category
ordinal, because the ratings are ordered but the gaps may not be equal
interval, because the numbers are evenly spaced from 1 to 5
ratio, because the scale has a true zero point below 1
questions.explanation: The ratings can be ranked, but there is no guarantee the difference between 'unhappy' and 'neutral' equals that between 'happy' and 'very happy', so the data are ordinal. The numbers being evenly spaced on paper does not make the underlying intervals equal.

questions.stem: Which variable is measured at the ratio level rather than the interval level?
options: the year in which each participant was born
reaction time in milliseconds
temperature in degrees Celsius
a ranking of finishing places in a race
questions.explanation: Ratio data have equal intervals and a true zero, so a reaction time of 400 ms is twice 200 ms. Celsius temperature and calendar years have equal intervals but no true zero, which makes them interval data; race places are ordinal.

questions.stem: A student surveys the first 20 people she meets in the school library. Which sampling procedure is this?
options: convenience sampling
random sampling
stratified sampling
random allocation
questions.explanation: Convenience sampling uses people who are easy to reach. It is quick but is unlikely to represent the population, because library users may differ from other students.

questions.stem: A sports club has 240 members: 180 adults and 60 juniors. A researcher wants a stratified sample of 40. How many juniors should be selected?
questions.explanation: Juniors are 60/240 = 25% of the club, so they should be 25% of the sample: 0.25 × 40 = 10. The remaining 30 participants would be adults, keeping each group in proportion.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the researcher lets participants choose whether to join the exercise group or the rest group. Those who choose exercise are generally fitter. What problem does this create, and how should it be fixed?
options: Fitness may confound the results; participants should be randomly allocated
The sample is too small; participants should be stratified by fitness level
The sample is too large; a convenience sample should be used instead
Fitness becomes the dependent variable; it should be measured twice
questions.explanation: Self-selection means the groups may differ in fitness as well as the independent variable, so fitness could explain any difference. Random allocation gives each participant an equal chance of being in either group, spreading participant variables evenly.

questions.stem: In a single-blind procedure:
options: participants do not know that they are taking part in a study at all
participants do not know which condition they are in
the researcher does not know which condition each participant is in
neither participants nor researcher know which condition each participant is in
questions.explanation: A single-blind procedure keeps participants unaware of their condition, controlling participant expectations such as the placebo effect. When the researcher is also unaware, the procedure is double-blind.

questions.stem: A double-blind procedure controls for which source of error that a single-blind procedure does not?
options: participants guessing the aim of the study and changing their behaviour
differences between participants in the two groups before the study begins
practice effects that occur when participants repeat the same task
the researcher's expectations influencing how participants behave or are scored
questions.explanation: In a double-blind procedure the person collecting the data does not know participants' conditions, so the experimenter effect is controlled as well as participant expectations. Differences between groups at the start are controlled by random allocation.

questions.stem: Why should every participant in an experiment receive the same written instructions, read in the same way?
options: Standardised procedures allow participants to choose their own condition
Standardised procedures remove the need for random allocation to conditions
Standardised procedures let the researcher know each participant's condition
Standardised procedures stop differences in instructions affecting the results
questions.explanation: If instructions or procedures varied, the difference could influence the dependent variable and act as an extraneous or confounding variable. Standardising them reduces this error and also allows the study to be replicated.

questions.stem: In a study of a new anxiety therapy, participants' anxiety levels fall in both the therapy group and a group given a convincing fake treatment. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A sampling error, as the groups were selected randomly
A placebo effect, as expectations alone reduced anxiety
An experimenter effect, as the researcher knew the conditions
An order effect, as participants completed both conditions
questions.explanation: When a fake treatment produces improvement, participants' expectations are likely to be responsible: the placebo effect. The real therapy is effective only if it improves anxiety more than the placebo does.

questions.stem: Which ethical principle requires that participants are told the nature, purpose and risks of a study before agreeing to take part?
options: debriefing
confidentiality
withdrawal rights
informed consent
questions.explanation: Informed consent means participants agree to take part only after being told what the study involves and any risks. For participants under 18, consent is also obtained from a parent or guardian.

questions.stem: After a study that used deception, the researcher explains its true purpose to participants and answers their questions. This is:
options: confidentiality
voluntary participation
debriefing
informed consent
questions.explanation: Debriefing occurs at the end of a study. Participants are told the true aims, any deception is explained, and any distress is addressed. Informed consent happens before the study begins.

questions.stem: A researcher stores participants' questionnaire answers under code numbers on a password-protected computer and never publishes their names. Which principle is this?
options: withdrawal rights
use of deception
confidentiality
debriefing
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects the privacy and security of participants' personal information, so they cannot be identified from published results. Withdrawal rights are about leaving a study without penalty.

questions.stem: When is the use of deception in psychological research acceptable?
options: Whenever the researcher believes participants would refuse to join if told the aim
When the participants are children, as they cannot understand the true aim of a study
Whenever the study is low risk, in which case debriefing is not needed afterwards
When knowing the true aim would change participants' behaviour, and a debriefing follows
questions.explanation: Deception is used only when telling participants the aim would bias their behaviour and the research could not be done another way, and participants must be fully debriefed afterwards. It is never a way around participants who would refuse, and debriefing is always required.

questions.stem: Partway through a study, a participant feels uncomfortable and asks to leave. The researcher should:
options: ask them to finish, because their consent at the start was voluntary
let them leave, but keep their data because it has already been collected
let them leave, but withhold any payment that they were promised
let them leave without penalty and remove their data if they request it
questions.explanation: Withdrawal rights allow participants to stop at any time without penalty and to have their data withdrawn. Agreeing at the start does not oblige them to continue, because participation must remain voluntary.

questions.stem: The scores of seven participants on a memory test are 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 25. What are the mean and median?
options: mean 7, median 5
mean 8, median 5
mean 5, median 8
mean 8, median 4
questions.explanation: The scores sum to 56, and 56 ÷ 7 = 8, so the mean is 8. In order, the middle (fourth) score is 5, so the median is 5. The mode is 4, which is not the median.

questions.stem: For the scores 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 25, which measure of central tendency best represents a typical score, and why?
options: The mean, because outliers have no effect on its value
The median, because the extreme score of 25 pulls the mean upwards
The mean, because it uses every score, including the score of 25
The median, because it is always larger than the mean for any data
questions.explanation: The outlier of 25 raises the mean to 8, above six of the seven scores. The median of 5 is not affected by how extreme the outlier is, so it better reflects a typical score here.

questions.stem: The interquartile range (IQR) of a data set is:
options: the spread of the middle 50% of scores, from Q1 to Q3
the difference between the highest and lowest scores
the average distance of the scores from the mean
the score that occurs most often in the data set
questions.explanation: IQR = Q3 - Q1, which covers the middle half of the data. Because it ignores the extreme quarter at each end, it is less affected by outliers than the range, which uses only the highest and lowest scores.

questions.stem: Two groups both have a mean anxiety score of 30. Group A has a standard deviation of 3 and Group B has a standard deviation of 9. What does this show?
options: Group A's results are more statistically significant than Group B's
Group B's scores are more spread out from the mean than Group A's
Group B has a higher average anxiety score than Group A
Group A's scores are more spread out from the mean than Group B's
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures how spread out scores are around the mean, so a larger value means greater variability. The means are equal, so neither group is more anxious on average.

questions.stem: A sample of 16 participants has a mean reaction time of 300 ms and a standard deviation of 12 ms. What is the standard error of the mean? Use SE = s/√n.
options: 48 ms
3 ms
12 ms
questions.explanation: SE = 12 ÷ √16 = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 ms. Dividing by 16 instead of its square root gives 0.75 ms, and multiplying by √16 gives 48 ms.

questions.stem: What happens to the standard error of the mean as the sample size increases, if the standard deviation stays the same?
options: It decreases, so the sample mean is a more precise estimate
It increases, so the sample mean is a more precise estimate
It decreases, so the sample mean is a less precise estimate
It stays the same, because it depends only on the mean
questions.explanation: Standard error is s/√n, so a larger sample gives a smaller standard error and a narrower confidence interval. The sample mean is then a more precise estimate of the population mean.

questions.stem: Mean recall in two conditions is shown on a column graph with 95% confidence interval error bars. The bars for the two conditions overlap a great deal. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The difference between the conditions may not be statistically significant
The difference between the conditions is certainly statistically significant
The two conditions had exactly the same population mean recall score
The study had no random errors, because the error bars were small
questions.explanation: A 95% confidence interval gives a range likely to contain the population mean. Heavily overlapping intervals suggest the true means may not differ, so the difference may not be significant, although a t-test is needed to decide. Overlap does not show the means are identical.

questions.stem: A Pearson correlation coefficient of r = -0.85 between hours of sleep and errors on a task shows:
options: a strong negative relationship: more sleep goes with fewer errors
a weak negative relationship: more sleep goes with fewer errors
a strong positive relationship: more sleep goes with more errors
that sleeping more causes people to make fewer errors
questions.explanation: Pearson r ranges from -1 to +1. A value close to -1 shows a strong negative relationship, where one variable rises as the other falls. Correlation alone cannot show that sleep causes the change in errors.

questions.stem: Which t-test is appropriate for comparing the scores of the same participants before and after a mindfulness program?
options: a paired t-test, because the two sets of scores come from the same people
an unpaired t-test, because the scores were collected at two different times
a paired t-test, because the participants were randomly allocated to groups
an unpaired t-test, because the program is the independent variable
questions.explanation: A paired t-test is used when each score in one condition is linked to a score in the other, as in repeated measures and matched participants designs. An unpaired t-test compares two separate, independent groups.

questions.stem: A study comparing two teaching methods reports p = 0.03. Using the conventional level of significance of 0.05, what should the researcher conclude?
options: There is a 3% chance that the alternative hypothesis is correct
The result proves the new method is better for every student
The result is significant, so the null hypothesis can be rejected
The result is not significant, so the null hypothesis is retained
questions.explanation: Because p = 0.03 is less than 0.05, a difference this large would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, so the result is significant and the null hypothesis is rejected. A p-value is not the probability that the alternative hypothesis is correct.

questions.stem: A researcher concludes that a new therapy reduces anxiety, but in reality it has no effect. What kind of error is this?
options: a type I error, retaining a null hypothesis that is false
a type II error, retaining a null hypothesis that is false
a type I error, rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
a type II error, rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
questions.explanation: A type I error is a false positive: finding an effect that does not really exist, by rejecting a true null hypothesis. A type II error is a false negative: missing a real effect by retaining a false null hypothesis.

questions.stem: A study with only 8 participants finds no significant difference between two conditions. Why should the researcher be cautious about concluding there is no effect?
options: With a small sample, a false effect is always found, a type I error
With a small sample, the mean cannot be calculated for each group
With a small sample, the p-value is always smaller than 0.05
With a small sample, a real effect may be missed, a type II error
questions.explanation: Small samples give large standard errors and little statistical power, so a genuine difference may fail to reach significance. Small samples can also violate the assumptions of inferential tests, adding uncertainty to the conclusion.

questions.stem: Two observers record aggressive acts in a playground video and their counts differ greatly. What would best improve the reliability of the observations?
options: Training both observers to use the same clear definition of aggression
Allowing each observer to define aggression in their own way
Increasing the number of children shown in the playground video
Telling the observers the hypothesis before they watch the video
questions.explanation: Reliability of observers improves when they are trained to use the same precise, operationalised categories, so they record the same behaviour consistently. Telling them the hypothesis risks bias rather than improving consistency.

questions.stem: A personality test gives very different scores when the same people complete it two weeks apart, although their personalities have not changed. This test lacks:
options: external validity
a control group
random sampling
reliability
questions.explanation: A reliable test produces consistent results when the same thing is measured again under the same conditions. Large changes in scores over two weeks show poor test-retest reliability.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes internal validity from external validity?
options: Internal is whether results generalise; external is whether the IV caused the change in the DV
Internal is whether results are consistent when repeated; external is whether the sample was large
Internal is whether results are consistent when repeated; external is whether a control group was used
Internal is whether the IV caused the change in the DV; external is whether results generalise
questions.explanation: A study is internally valid if the change in the dependent variable was caused by the independent variable and not by confounding variables. It is externally valid if its results generalise to other people, settings and times. Consistency of results is reliability.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of peer review in psychological research?
options: The researcher's colleagues repeat the study to obtain identical results
A government body decides which studies may be carried out in a country
Independent experts check a study's methods and conclusions before publication
Participants check the researcher's conclusions before the study is published
questions.explanation: In peer review, other experts in the field evaluate a study's design, analysis and conclusions before a journal publishes it, helping to catch errors and unjustified claims. Repeating a study is replication, which is a separate process.
